title: Containers & Docker
scopeHtml:
Scope: containers vs VMs, image layers and Dockerfiles, tags and digests, container security, Compose.

Scope: runtime internals, networking, volumes, BuildKit, debugging and JVM memory.

notes.title: Why containers
notes.html:
A container packages an app with everything it needs (runtime, libraries, config files) so it runs the same everywhere. It is not a small VM: containers share the host's Linux kernel and are isolated using namespaces (what a process can see: its own PIDs, network, filesystem) and cgroups (how much CPU/memory it may use). A VM carries a whole guest OS (GBs, minutes to boot); a container is MBs and starts in under a second.

VM:         App | Libs | Guest OS | Hypervisor | Host OS | Hardware
Container:  App | Libs | Container runtime | Host OS (shared kernel) | Hardware

Worked example. A host with 64 GB RAM fits ~8 VMs of 8 GB each, but could run 100+ containers of 300 MB, which is why companies pack services densely and save money.

Industry examples. Google ran containers (via cgroups) for years before Docker; Spotify, Uber and Airbnb run thousands of services as containers on Kubernetes.

Everyday analogy. Apartments in one building share plumbing and electricity (kernel) but each has its own locked door and meter. A VM is a separate house with its own plumbing.

Common interview traps.

  • "Containers are lightweight VMs": they share the kernel, so a kernel exploit or a Linux-only image does not run on Windows without a VM layer.
  • Assuming containers are a security boundary as strong as VMs.

notes.title: Images, layers and the Dockerfile
notes.html:
An image is a read-only template made of stacked layers; each Dockerfile instruction (FROM, COPY, RUN...) creates a layer. A container is a running instance of an image plus a thin writable layer. Layers are cached by content: if an instruction and everything before it is unchanged, Docker reuses the layer.

So order matters: put things that change rarely first.

FROM node:22-slim AS build        # stage 1: has compilers and dev tools
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./             # dependency manifest first
RUN npm ci                        # cached until package*.json changes
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM node:22-slim                 # stage 2: small runtime image
WORKDIR /app
ENV NODE_ENV=production
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
COPY --from=build /app/node_modules ./node_modules
USER node                         # do not run as root
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]

This is a multi-stage build: build tools stay in stage 1, the final image has only what runs (often 1 GB down to 150 MB).

Industry examples. Google's distroless images and Alpine variants shrink attack surface; Cloud Native Buildpacks and Jib (Java) build images without a Dockerfile.

Everyday analogy. A sandwich: bread and filling layers; if only the top slice changes you don't remake the whole sandwich.

Common interview traps.

  • COPY . . before npm ci: every code change busts the dependency cache.
  • latest tag in FROM: unreproducible builds.
  • Secrets passed with ARG or COPY remain readable in image layers.

notes.title: Tags, digests and registries
notes.html:
A registry (Docker Hub, GitHub Container Registry, Amazon ECR, Google Artifact Registry) stores images. An image name is registry/repo:tag. A tag is a movable label (:1.4.2, :latest); a digest (@sha256:...) is the immutable content hash.

Production should deploy by digest or by an immutable tag such as the git commit SHA, never latest: latest can silently point to something else, so two nodes can run different code under the same name.

Typical flow in CI: build once → tag with commit SHA → push → scan → deploy that exact digest. Also set retention policies, since registries fill with thousands of old images.

Industry examples. Netflix "bakes" immutable images (AMIs) per release; AWS ECR offers tag immutability and image scanning.

Everyday analogy. A tag is a sticky note saying "current menu"; a digest is a photo of the exact menu. Sticky notes get moved; photos do not.

Common interview traps.

  • Using :latest in a Kubernetes manifest: a rollback cannot tell what "previous" was.
  • Public base images pulled unverified; pin and scan them.

notes.title: Container security basics
notes.html:
The usual hardening list:

  • Run as a non-root user; drop Linux capabilities; use a read-only root filesystem where possible.
  • Small base image (slim/distroless) = fewer CVEs.
  • Scan images for known vulnerabilities (Trivy, Grype, Snyk, ECR scanning) in CI and again on a schedule, since new CVEs appear after you ship.
  • Never bake secrets into the image; inject at runtime.
  • Sign images (cosign/Sigstore) and verify signatures before deploy; generate an SBOM (list of components).

Worked example. A node:18 image from last year has 140 known CVEs, 5 critical; rebuilding on node:22-slim and removing unused packages drops it to 12 with none critical.

Industry examples. Log4Shell (Dec 2021) showed why teams needed SBOMs: they had to find every image containing a vulnerable Log4j in hours.

Everyday analogy. Checking food ingredients against a recall list: you need to know exactly what went in.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing "it's in a container so it's isolated" while running privileged or mounting the Docker socket.

notes.title: Docker Compose and local development
notes.html:
Docker Compose describes several containers (app, database, cache) in one YAML file so docker compose up gives a developer a full stack. It is for local dev and tests, not for production orchestration (that is Kubernetes' job).

services:
  api:
    build: .
    ports: ["8080:8080"]
    environment:
      DB_URL: postgres://app:app@db:5432/app
    depends_on:
      db: { condition: service_healthy }
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    environment: { POSTGRES_PASSWORD: app, POSTGRES_USER: app, POSTGRES_DB: app }
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U app"]
      interval: 5s
    volumes: [dbdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data]
volumes:
  dbdata:

Volumes keep data outside the container's lifetime (containers are disposable). Use the same compose file in CI to run integration tests against real Postgres/Redis (or use Testcontainers).

Industry examples. Testcontainers (Java, Go, Node) spins real dependencies per test run; many teams run it in CI for realistic tests.

Everyday analogy. A meal-kit box: everything for one dinner, ready to unpack and cook with one step.

Common interview traps.

  • Storing database data in the container's writable layer: it disappears when the container is removed.
  • depends_on waits only for start, not for readiness, unless a health check is used.

notes.title: Inside the runtime: OCI, containerd, runc
notes.html:
"Docker" is really several layers. The OCI (Open Container Initiative) specs define the image format and runtime. containerd manages images and container lifecycles; runc is the low-level tool that actually creates the process using Linux kernel features. Kubernetes talks to a runtime through the CRI and today usually uses containerd or CRI-O directly (Docker the daemon is not required on nodes).

Kernel building blocks: namespaces (pid, net, mnt, uts, ipc, user) isolate what a process sees; cgroups limit CPU, memory, I/O; overlayfs stacks image layers as one filesystem; seccomp/AppArmor restrict system calls.

Worked example. docker run --memory=256m sets a cgroup memory limit; allocating past it makes the kernel OOM-kill the container's process (exit code 137).

Industry examples. Kubernetes removed "dockershim" in v1.24, so clusters run containerd or CRI-O; AWS Fargate uses Firecracker microVMs for stronger isolation.

Everyday analogy. The Docker command is the restaurant waiter; containerd is the kitchen manager; runc is the cook who actually makes the dish.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying Kubernetes "removed Docker support" means images stopped working. Images are OCI-standard and still run.
  • Exit code 137 = killed by SIGKILL, often OOM; not an application bug per se.

notes.title: Container networking
notes.html:
Each container gets its own network namespace. The default bridge network connects containers on one host through a virtual switch with NAT; -p 8080:80 publishes a container port on the host. Containers on a user-defined network reach each other by name via built-in DNS. host networking shares the host's stack (fast, no isolation).

In Kubernetes a CNI plugin (Calico, Cilium, Flannel, AWS VPC CNI) gives every pod its own IP, and pods can reach each other without NAT. Services provide stable virtual IPs and DNS names (orders.shop.svc.cluster.local).

Worked example. App container cannot reach localhost:5432 for Postgres: inside the container localhost is the container itself. Use the Compose service name db:5432.

Industry examples. Cilium (eBPF) is used by Google GKE Dataplane V2 and many large clusters for networking and policy.

Everyday analogy. Apartments in a building each have their own internal phone extension (container network); the main reception number (published port) routes visitors in.

Common interview traps.

  • Using localhost to reach another container.
  • Publishing a database port to 0.0.0.0 on a public host.

notes.title: Volumes and persistent data
notes.html:
A container's writable layer is ephemeral: gone when the container is removed. Persist data with volumes (managed by Docker, best for databases) or bind mounts (a host directory, handy in development), or tmpfs (memory only). In Kubernetes use PersistentVolumes via claims and StatefulSets for databases.

Good practice: containers should be stateless and disposable; keep state in managed services (RDS, Redis, S3). Back up volumes; know the filesystem permissions problem when running as non-root.

Worked example. A team stored uploads in the container filesystem. Each deploy replaced the pod and users' files vanished. Moving uploads to object storage fixed it and allowed horizontal scaling.

Industry examples. Most companies run databases outside Kubernetes (managed cloud DBs) or via mature operators (Zalando Postgres Operator, Strimzi for Kafka).

Everyday analogy. A hotel room is cleaned for each guest (container); valuables go in the safe at reception (volume).

Common interview traps.

  • Writing important data to the container filesystem.
  • Running stateful systems with multiple replicas sharing one ReadWriteOnce volume.

notes.title: Build performance and BuildKit
notes.html:
BuildKit (the default builder in modern Docker) builds independent stages in parallel, caches smarter, and supports cache mounts, secret mounts and SSH forwarding.

# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.m2 mvn -q package      # reuse the Maven cache across builds
RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npmrc,target=/root/.npmrc npm ci  # secret never lands in a layer

In CI, layers do not persist between ephemeral runners, so export and import the cache (--cache-to/--cache-from type=registry or the GitHub Actions cache). Also use .dockerignore, pin base image digests, and build multi-architecture images (buildx) when you deploy to both amd64 and arm64 (Graviton saves money).

Worked example. A 9-minute image build drops to 90 seconds with a registry cache and a Maven cache mount when only application code changed.

Industry examples. Buildpacks, Jib, Kaniko (rootless builds in Kubernetes) and Bazel's rules_oci are alternatives where Docker-in-Docker is a concern.

Everyday analogy. Keeping chopped onions in the fridge between dinners instead of starting from whole onions every night.

Common interview traps.

  • Docker-in-Docker with --privileged on shared runners; prefer Kaniko or BuildKit rootless.
  • Building only amd64 and then deploying to arm64 nodes.

notes.title: Debugging containers and JVM memory
notes.html:
Core commands: docker logs -f, docker exec -it <id> sh, docker inspect, docker stats; in Kubernetes kubectl logs, exec, and ephemeral debug containers (kubectl debug) for distroless images that have no shell.

JVM in containers: modern JVMs read container limits (-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75), but heap is not total memory: metaspace, thread stacks, direct buffers and the JIT also count. With a 512 MiB limit and -Xmx512m, the container will be OOM-killed (exit 137). Leave headroom (heap about 60-75% of the limit). Also tune GC threads to the CPU limit, and handle SIGTERM for graceful shutdown.

Worked example. Pod restarts every ~4 hours with OOMKilled, yet heap dumps look fine. Native memory (thread stacks and direct buffers) pushed total use above the 512 MiB limit; raising the limit to 768 MiB and setting MaxRAMPercentage=65 fixed it.

Industry examples. Netflix and others publish JVM-in-container tuning guides; Spring Boot and Quarkus ship container-aware defaults.

Everyday analogy. A suitcase with a weight limit: the clothes (heap) are not the only weight; the suitcase and shoes (non-heap) count too.

Common interview traps.

  • Setting -Xmx equal to the container limit.
  • Opening a shell in production containers as the normal way to debug instead of logs, metrics and traces.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html: Containers package an app with its dependencies and share the host kernel, isolated by namespaces and cgroups, so they are small and start fast. Images are layered and cached; order Dockerfile steps from rarely to frequently changing and use multi-stage builds for small runtime images. Deploy immutable tags or digests, never latest. Harden with non-root users, slim bases, vulnerability scans, signing and SBOMs, and keep secrets out of layers. Use Compose for local and CI stacks, volumes for persistent data.

questions.promptHtml: What is a container and how is it different from a virtual machine?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The most basic infrastructure question; shallow answers show up immediately.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A container is an isolated process that shares the host's kernel. Linux namespaces limit what it can see (processes, network, filesystem) and cgroups limit what it can use (CPU, memory). A VM runs a full guest OS on a hypervisor, so it is heavier and slower to start.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Containers start in under a second and are MBs; VMs are GBs and take longer. Isolation is weaker: all containers share one kernel, so a kernel exploit matters more. Hence the use of non-root users, seccomp profiles, and sandboxed runtimes (gVisor, Kata) for untrusted code.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "A container is a lightweight VM."
  • Assuming a Linux image runs natively on Windows or macOS (Docker Desktop uses a hidden Linux VM).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does cgroups do? → Enforce resource limits and accounting.
  2. When pick a VM? → Strong isolation, different kernels or OS.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior states the shared-kernel security implication.

questions.promptHtml: How does Docker layer caching work, and how would you structure a Dockerfile for fast rebuilds and a small image?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Slow, huge images are a very common real problem.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Each instruction makes a layer cached by its content and everything above it. Put rarely changing steps first (base image, dependency install) and frequently changing steps last (copy source). Use multi-stage builds so compilers and dev tools stay in the build stage and the final image holds only what runs.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Copying package*.json and running npm ci before COPY . . means source edits do not invalidate the dependency layer. A .dockerignore keeps junk out of the build context. Final image: slim or distroless base, USER non-root, HEALTHCHECK optional. Multi-stage often cuts 1 GB to 150 MB.

FROM node:22-slim AS build
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build
FROM node:22-slim
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
USER node
CMD ["node","dist/server.js"]

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• COPY . . first, busting the cache on every change.
  • Secrets passed via ARG/COPY remain in layers.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why multi-stage? → Smaller image, fewer CVEs, no build tools in prod.
  2. How do you build with a secret? → BuildKit --mount=type=secret.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior mentions BuildKit cache mounts, reproducibility and base image pinning.

questions.promptHtml: Why should you not deploy the latest tag to production?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Immutability and rollback are core release-safety ideas.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A tag is a movable label. latest can point to different images over time, so two nodes may run different code under the same name and you cannot tell what to roll back to. Deploy an immutable tag such as the commit SHA, or the content digest @sha256:....

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: A digest is a hash of the image manifest, so it cannot change. Registries (ECR, GAR, GHCR) can enforce tag immutability. Kubernetes imagePullPolicy and a node cache add further confusion with mutable tags. Add retention policies so old images do not accumulate forever.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Rollback by "redeploy latest".
  • Tags like v1 re-pushed over the old one.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you tie a running pod to source? → Tag with commit SHA, add OCI labels.
  2. How to verify integrity? → Sign with cosign and verify at admission.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior adds signing, admission control and provenance.

questions.promptHtml: List practical steps to harden a container image and its runtime.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Security baselines expected at 3 YOE.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Small base image (slim or distroless), run as non-root, drop capabilities and use a read-only filesystem, scan images in CI and on a schedule, keep secrets out of the image, sign images and generate an SBOM.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Smaller images have fewer packages and therefore fewer CVEs. Scheduled rescans matter because new CVEs appear after a release. Kubernetes adds securityContext (runAsNonRoot, readOnlyRootFilesystem, allowPrivilegeEscalation: false) and admission policies. Never mount the Docker socket into a container: it is root on the host.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Running --privileged for convenience.
  • Scanning only at build time.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is an SBOM for? → Quickly answer "which images contain library X" (Log4Shell).
  2. What is distroless? → Image with only the app and runtime, no shell or package manager.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior mentions admission policies, signing and supply-chain provenance.

questions.promptHtml: Your integration tests need Postgres and Redis. How do you run them in CI, and what happens to the data when the container stops?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests practical CI design and volume understanding.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Use Docker Compose or Testcontainers to start real Postgres and Redis for the test run. Data in a container's writable layer disappears when the container is removed; for tests that is desirable, and anything that must persist uses a named volume.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Add health checks and wait for readiness (depends_on: condition: service_healthy), because "started" is not "ready". Testcontainers gives per-test-class isolation and random ports, avoiding clashes between parallel jobs. Compose is for local development and tests, not production orchestration.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Fixed host ports clashing with parallel CI jobs.
  • Tests assuming the database is ready as soon as the container starts.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Mocks vs real DB? → Real dependencies catch migration and SQL-dialect bugs mocks hide.
  2. How do you keep it fast? → Reuse containers per suite, in-memory tmpfs for data.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior balances realism with speed and uses disposable, isolated data.

questions.contextHtml: A Java service image is 1.4 GB. Pulling it on a fresh Kubernetes node takes ~90 seconds, so autoscaling reacts slowly during traffic spikes. The Dockerfile uses FROM ubuntu, installs the JDK and Maven, copies the repo and runs mvn package inside the final image. Every commit rebuilds all layers (11 minutes).
questions.promptHtml: How would you fix both image size and build time?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Compress the image or delete files in a later RUN; deleted files still exist in earlier layers.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which Java version? Native or JVM? How often do dependencies change? Is there a registry in the same region as the cluster?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Pre-pull images on nodes or keep warm capacity for spikes.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Build tools in runtime image; no layer ordering; large base; no .dockerignore.
  4. How I'd verify: docker history and dive to see layer sizes; build timings.
  5. Root cause: A single-stage build with a heavy base and dependency download after copying source.
  6. Fix: Multi-stage build: Maven stage with dependency resolution cached (copy pom.xml first, or BuildKit cache mount), final stage on a JRE-slim or distroless base with a layered jar (Spring Boot layers) or Jib; run non-root.
  7. Prevention: Size budget check in CI, scheduled base-image updates.
  8. Trade-offs: Distroless has no shell for debugging (use ephemeral debug containers); native image reduces size more but lengthens builds.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Startup time still slow? → JVM flags, CDS/AppCDS, or GraalVM native image.
  • Multiple services share a base? → Standard internal base image maintained by the platform team.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team cut image size from 1.2 GB to 180 MB and scale-out latency from 2 minutes to 25 seconds, which stopped a recurring brown-out at traffic peaks.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tries cleanup commands in the same layer chain without understanding layers.
  • Hire: multi-stage, slim base, cache ordering.
  • Strong hire: measures with dive, handles caching in CI, security and debugging trade-offs.

questions.promptHtml: What are namespaces and cgroups, and what do containerd and runc do?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates users of Docker from people who understand it.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Namespaces isolate what a process can see (PIDs, network, mounts, hostname, users); cgroups limit what it can use (CPU, memory, I/O). runc is the low-level tool that creates a container process from an OCI spec; containerd manages images and container lifecycle and is what Kubernetes uses through the CRI.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Overlayfs stacks image layers; seccomp and AppArmor restrict system calls. Kubernetes removed dockershim in v1.24, but images still run because they are OCI-standard. Exceeding the memory cgroup gets the process OOM-killed (exit code 137).

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "Kubernetes dropped Docker, so images broke."
  • Treating exit code 137 as an application bug rather than a kill signal, often OOM.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is the CRI? → Kubernetes' interface to container runtimes.
  2. How do you get stronger isolation? → gVisor, Kata or Firecracker microVMs.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior connects the primitives to limits, OOM and isolation strength.

questions.promptHtml: Your app container cannot reach Postgres at localhost:5432 even though the database container is running. Why?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A very common beginner trap.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Each container has its own network namespace, so localhost inside the app container is the app container itself. Put both on the same user-defined network and connect using the service name, for example db:5432, resolved by Docker's built-in DNS.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: The default bridge network uses NAT; -p host:container publishes a port on the host. Host networking shares the host stack with no isolation. In Kubernetes every pod gets its own IP and Services give stable DNS names.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using localhost to reach another container.
  • Publishing a database port to the public interface.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does a published port expose the database to the internet? → If bound to 0.0.0.0 on a public host, yes.
  2. Compose service names? → They become DNS hostnames on the Compose network.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior mentions CNI, Services and network policy for production.

questions.promptHtml: After each deployment users' uploaded files disappear. What is wrong and how do you fix it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Statelessness is key to scaling containers.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Files were written to the container's ephemeral writable layer, which is deleted when the pod is replaced. Keep containers stateless: store uploads in object storage like S3, data in managed databases, and use volumes or persistent volumes only for state that must live on disk.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Volumes are managed by the runtime; bind mounts map host directories (development); tmpfs is memory only. Multiple replicas cannot share one ReadWriteOnce volume. Databases in Kubernetes need StatefulSets, backups and failover, or a managed service.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Writing important data to the container filesystem.
  • Several replicas fighting over one single-writer volume.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why object storage? → Scales horizontally, durable, decoupled from pods.
  2. Permission errors on volumes? → Non-root user needs matching ownership (fsGroup).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior prefers managed stateful services and designs backup and restore.

questions.promptHtml: How do you speed up Docker builds in CI where runners are ephemeral?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Layer caches do not survive fresh runners.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Use BuildKit with a remote cache (--cache-from/--cache-to to a registry or the CI cache), order the Dockerfile so dependency layers are stable, use cache mounts for package managers, add a .dockerignore, and build multi-stage so only changed stages rebuild. Use secret mounts so credentials never land in layers.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: BuildKit builds independent stages in parallel. For multi-architecture images use buildx. Avoid Docker-in-Docker with --privileged on shared runners; prefer rootless BuildKit or Kaniko.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Privileged Docker-in-Docker on shared runners.
  • Building only amd64 then deploying to arm64 nodes.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you pin the base image? → By digest, updated by Renovate.
  2. Alternative to Dockerfiles? → Buildpacks or Jib.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior combines caching, security and multi-arch.

questions.contextHtml: A Java service runs in Kubernetes with a 512 MiB memory limit and -Xmx512m. Pods restart about every 4 hours with OOMKilled (exit 137). Heap dumps taken before the kill look healthy at ~380 MiB. CPU is normal and the restarts cause brief error spikes.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "There is a memory leak in the app" without noticing the heap is nowhere near the limit.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: JVM version and flags? Thread count? Direct buffer use (Netty)? Is MaxRAMPercentage set?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Raise the limit (for example to 768 MiB) and lower heap so the service stops flapping.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Total JVM memory (heap + metaspace + thread stacks + direct buffers + code cache) exceeds the limit; native leak; too many threads.
  4. How I'd verify: -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary, jcmd VM.native_memory, container memory metrics, thread count.
  5. Root cause: Xmx equal to the container limit leaves no room for non-heap memory.
  6. Fix: Set -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=60-70, size the limit with headroom, cap threads and direct memory.
  7. Prevention: Load test with production limits, alert on memory working set versus limit, and dashboards for heap and non-heap.
  8. Trade-offs: Higher limits cost money; right-size with real measurements.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Exit code 137 but no OOM in logs → kernel cgroup OOM, check kubectl describe Last State.
  • Would CPU limits matter? → Throttling can hurt latency and GC.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A fix to MaxRAMPercentage plus a 256 MiB larger limit ended weekly restart pages with no code changes.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames a leak with no evidence.
  • Hire: understands non-heap memory and fixes limits.
  • Strong hire: uses NMT, load tests and alerts on working set.
